memory_update.text: ECVT should remain a priority underfollowed candidate for sulphuric-acid chokepoint work because it is a U.S.-listed small-cap with direct sulfuric acid recycling/regeneration and virgin acid production exposure.

HWKN is a weaker but useful discovery-lane hypothesis: it handles sulfuric acid as part of Industrial Solutions bulk chemical distribution, but acid-specific revenue, margin and allocation exposure must be verified before promotion.
MOS and FCX are reference anchors rather than underfollowed alpha candidates: they demonstrate downstream dependence on sulfur/sulfuric acid in phosphate fertilizers and copper SX-EW/leaching.

Need a separate pass for logistics/storage/tank-car/tanker names such as regulated liquid-bulk transport and acid storage assets; this Layer 1B pass found distributor exposure but did not fully map physical acid logistics.

ECVT should be retained as the cleanest US-listed underfollowed candidate for the sulphuric-acid node because its remaining core business is directly tied to virgin sulphuric acid, regeneration services and sulphuric-acid derivatives.
LXU should be retained as a small-cap industrial-acid/mining-input candidate, but later layers must verify sulphuric-acid revenue share and external merchant exposure before upgrading it.

KEX belongs in a speculative second-order logistics lane, not the direct acid-supplier lane, until specific sulphuric-acid, spent-acid, molten-sulphur or corrosive-chemical transport exposure is verified.

MOS is useful as a reference demand anchor: sulphur scarcity can pressure phosphate fertilizer economics through molten-sulphur-to-sulphuric-acid conversion, but MOS is not a pure bottleneck supplier.

Need a dedicated non-US or ADR/OTC pass for smelter-acid exporters in Japan, Korea, Canada and Europe; the US-listed universe may miss the most direct Asian smelter-acid beneficiaries referenced by Kpler.

Need a follow-up equipment pass for acid-resistant tanks, pumps, linings, heat exchangers, acid plants and EPC vendors; this pass found clearer US-listed chemical/logistics names than acid-equipment pure plays.

HWKN is the cleanest US-listed underfollowed distributor candidate found so far: explicit sulphuric-acid product catalog plus 10-K language on receiving, storing and distributing sulphuric acid, but revenue sensitivity remains unproven.

KEX should be tracked as a logistics hypothesis, not a proven acid play: it is a dominant US tank-barge operator for bulk liquids/agricultural chemicals, but direct sulphuric-acid cargo exposure must be verified before upgrading.
CECO is a niche acid-plant equipment/services hypothesis via mist eliminators and corrosion-resistant process-gas systems used in sulphuric-acid and phosphate-fertilizer industries.

Smelter-acid byproduct flows may be more investable through equipment, logistics and distribution names than through headline copper/nickel miners; Teck's Trail Operations is a useful North American reference asset for this mapping.

Need a follow-up pass on US-listed/OTC chemical tanker, storage terminal, corrosion-resistant tank/vessel, and non-US ADR names; several likely pure-play acid logistics beneficiaries may be foreign-listed or OTC and were not fully mapped in this pass.

HWKN is the cleanest underfollowed US-listed direct sulfuric-acid distributor candidate found in this pass; later layers should test revenue materiality, supplier access, storage capacity and margin pass-through.

KEX is a logistics-adjacent hypothesis, not yet proven sulfuric-acid exposure; it should survive only if later evidence confirms acid or acid-adjacent chemical cargo relevance, barge compatibility and contract repricing upside.

KBR is an acid-processing technology hypothesis tied to recovery, reconcentration and purification capex; later work must verify sulfuric-acid-specific backlog or awards before treating it as a real bottleneck owner.
Southern Copper and the provided Kpler evidence validate the node: sulfuric acid is both an input to copper leaching/SX-EW and a smelter byproduct that can be sold into mining and fertilizer markets.

US-listed pure-play sulphuric-acid logistics, storage and smelter-acid exporters appear scarce; many likely operators are private, foreign-listed, OTC, or embedded inside broader chemical/mining/logistics firms.

node: Sulphur and sulphuric-acid feedstock for copper SX-EW, nickel HPAL and fertilizers
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expansion found two reference anchors and two underfollowed U.S.-listed discovery candidates. Reference anchors are large direct customers or integrated users of sulphur/sulphuric acid: Mosaic in phosphate fertilizers and Freeport-McMoRan in copper leaching/SX-EW. Underfollowed candidates are closer to the acid supply/distribution layer: Ecovyst as a North American sulphuric-acid recycler/virgin acid producer, and Hawkins as a specialty chemical distributor that explicitly stores and distributes sulphuric acid. The strongest node exposure among small/mid-cap names is ECVT; HWKN is a distribution/logistics hypothesis that needs product-level margin and regional tightness verification. Layer 1B expands the US-listed universe around the sulphur/sulphuric-acid chokepoint. The most directly relevant underfollowed public names found in this pass are Ecovyst for virgin/regenerated sulphuric acid and LSB Industries for industrial sulphuric acid plus mining/industrial chemical adjacency. Kirby is a second-order logistics hypothesis because it controls a large US liquid-bulk tank-barge network for chemicals and agricultural chemicals, but specific sulphuric-acid cargo exposure still needs verification. Mosaic is included as a reference/context anchor rather than an alpha-discovery name: it is a large fertilizer producer that makes sulphuric acid internally from molten sulphur and is therefore exposed to sulphur feedstock availability and cost rather than being a pure bottleneck owner.
